metadata.title: A new approach to strong convergence

nodes.statement: A \emph{dart} $d$ in a graph $G$ is an oriented edge, meaning it has a start point $\mathrm{start}(d)$, and endpoint $\mathrm{end}(d)$, is carried by an edge $\mathrm{edge}(d)$, and, in the case where $e$ is a loop, it has an additional information encoded in a boolean $\in \{0, 1\}$ encoding an orientation. We denote as $D(G)$ the set of darts on $G$.
nodes.label: def:dart

nodes.statement: To each dart $d$ we associate a \emph{reverse dart} $\mathrm{rev}(d)$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathrm{start}(\mathrm{rev}(d)) = \mathrm{end}(d)$; \item $\mathrm{end}(\mathrm{rev}(d)) = \mathrm{start}(d)$; \item $\mathrm{edge}(\mathrm{rev}(d)) = \mathrm{edge}(d)$; \item if $\mathrm{edge}(d)$ is a loop then the orientation of $\mathrm{rev}(d)$ is the negation of the orientation of $d$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:reverse_dart

nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item For any dart $d$, $\mathrm{rev}(d) \neq d$. \item For any dart $d$, $\mathrm{rev}(\mathrm{rev}(d)) = d$. \item We have a map $e \in E(G) \mapsto d_e \in D(G)$ such that, for all $e$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$, then $d_e$ is a dart from $x$ to $y$ carried by $e$. \item For any $d, d'$, if $\mathrm{edge}(d)=\mathrm{edge}(d')$ then $d=d'$ or $d=\mathrm{rev}(d')$. \item We have $d_1 = d_2$ iff $\mathrm{start}(d_1) = \mathrm{start}(d_2)$ and $\mathrm{edge}(d_1) = \mathrm{edge}(d_2)$ (and same characterisation using the endpoints and edges). \end{itemize}
nodes.label: lem:dart_API

nodes.statement: These depend on the implementation of darts, but should be easily verified.
Let $x \in V(G)$. The \emph{dartset} of $x$ is the set \begin{equation} \mathrm{dartSet}(x) := \{ d \in D(G) \, : \, \mathrm{start}(d)=x\}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: def:dartset

nodes.statement: Let $x$, $y \in V(G)$. We define the dartset of $(x,y)$ as \begin{equation*} \mathrm{dartSet}(x,y) = \{ d \in D(G) : \mathrm{start}(d) = x, \mathrm{end}(d) = y\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:dartset_pair

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $x$ and $y$ are adjacent; \item there exists $d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)$ such that $\mathrm{end}(d)=y$; \item $\mathrm{dartSet}(x,y)$ is not empty. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:adjacent_vs_dart

nodes.statement: Trivial.

Let $x, y \in V(G)$. The map \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \mathrm{dartSet}(x,y) & \rightarrow E(G) \\ d & \mapsto \mathrm{edge}(d) \end{split} \end{equation*} has range $\{e \in E(G) : e \text{ links } x \text{ and } y\}$. It is $2-1$ if $x=y$ and $1-1$ otherwise.
nodes.label: lem:edge_range_of_darset

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set. A \emph{dart-like structure} on $V$ is the data of a set of darts $D$, together with maps $\mathrm{start}, \mathrm{end} : D \rightarrow V$ and $\mathrm{rev} : D \rightarrow D$ satisfying the following: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathrm{start} \circ \mathrm{rev} = \mathrm{end}$ and $\mathrm{end} \circ \mathrm{rev} = \mathrm{start}$; \item $\mathrm{rev}$ is an involution with no fixed point. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:dartlike

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set and $D$, $\mathrm{start}, \mathrm{end}, \mathrm{rev}$ be a dart-like structure. We define a relation on $D$ by: \begin{equation*} \forall d, d' \in D, \quad d \sim d' \Leftrightarrow (d=d' \text{ or } d = \mathrm{rev}(d')). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:dart_eq_rel

nodes.statement: The relation $\sim$ on $D$ is an equivalence relation, and all of its equivalence classes are of the form $\{d, \mathrm{rev}(d)\}$ (the two of which are distinct).
nodes.label: lem:dart_eq_rel

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set and $D$, $\mathrm{start}, \mathrm{end}, \mathrm{rev}$ be a dart-like structure. We define a graph $G$ associated to this structure by taking: \begin{itemize} \item $V(G) := V$ as the vertex set; \item $E(G) := D(G) \diagup \sim$ as the edge set; \item for $e \in E(G)$, if $d \in D(G)$ is a representant of $e$, then $e$ links $\mathrm{start}(d)$ and $\mathrm{end}(d)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:graph_of_dart

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ constructed in Definition \ref{def:graph_of_dart} is a graph, and $D(G) = D$.
nodes.label: thm:dart_of_graph_of_dart

nodes.statement: A \emph{subgraph} $H$ of $G$ is a graph (of the same type as $G$) defined by: \begin{itemize} \item a vertex set $V(H)$ included in the vextex set of $G$ \item an edge set $E(H)$ included in the edge set of $H$ \item the same $\mathrm{IsLink}$ relation, i.e. if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $H$ then it also links $x$ and $y$ in $G$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:subgraph

nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a subgraph of $G$. For any $x$, $y$ in $V(H)$, if $x$ and $y$ are adjacent for $H$, then they are adjacent for $G$.
nodes.label: lem:subgraph_adj_graph

nodes.statement: We define the \emph{union} $H_1 \cup H_2$ of two subgraphs by taking the union of their respective vertex sets and edge sets, and the intersection $H_1 \cap H_2$ by taking their intersection.
nodes.label: def:max_subgraph

nodes.statement: A subgraph $H$ of $G$ is \emph{induced} if, for any $x, y \in V(H)$, for any $e \in E(G)$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $G$, then $e \in E(H)$.
nodes.label: def:isinduced

nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a subset of $V(G)$. Then we define a subgraph $H$ induced by $U$ by letting: \begin{itemize} \item $V(H) := U$; \item $E(H) := \{ e \in E(G) : \text{ both endpoints of }e \text{ lie in } U\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:induced_subgraph

nodes.statement: A subgraph is induced iff it is induced from as subset of $V(G)$.
nodes.label: lem:induced_iff_isinduced

nodes.statement: A graph $G$ is \emph{finite} if $V(G)$ and $E(G)$ are both finite sets.
nodes.label: def:finite

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. We say $G$ is \emph{locally finite} at $x$ if $\mathrm{dartSet} (x)$ is finite. The graph $G$ is \emph{locally finite} if it is locally finite at every vertex.
nodes.label: def:locally_finite

nodes.statement: Let $x$ be a vertex of $G$. The \emph{edegree} of $x$ is defined as $\mathrm{edeg}(x) = \# \mathrm{dartSet}(x)$, which is an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$. The \emph{degree} of $x$ is the natural-number projection of the edegree.
nodes.label: def:degree

nodes.statement: If $G$ is locally finite at $x \in V(G)$, then $\# \mathrm{dartSet}(x,x)$ is an even number.
nodes.label: lem:darset_loop_even

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. $G$ is locally finite at $x$ iff $\mathrm{incidenceSet}(x)$ is finite, and in this case, \begin{equation*} \deg(x) = \# \mathrm{incidenceSet}(x) + \mathrm{loopSet}(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:degree_inc_loop

nodes.statement: Using Lemma \ref{lem:edge_range_of_darset}, \begin{align*} \deg(x) & = \sum_{y \in V(G)} \# \mathrm{dartSet}(x,y) \\ & = 2 \# \{e \in E(G) : e \text{ links }x,x\} + \sum_{y \in V(G), y \neq x} \# \{e \in E(G) : e \text{ links }x,y\}\\ & = 2 \# \mathrm{loopSet}(x) + (\# \mathrm{incidenceSet}(x) - \# \mathrm{loopSet}(x)) \end{align*} which leads to the desired equality. Hence $G$ is locally finite at $x$ iff $\mathrm{incidenceSet}(x)$ and $\mathrm{loopSet}(x)$ are both finite, which is equivalent to $\mathrm{incidenceSet}(x)$ being finite as $\mathrm{loopSet}(x) \subseteq \mathrm{incidenceSet}(x)$.
Let $\delta$ be a non-negative integer. We say $G$ is \emph{regular of degree $\delta$} if it is not empty, locally finite and, for every $x \in V(G)$, $\deg (x) = \delta$.
nodes.label: def:regular

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is regular of degree $0$ iff $E(G)=\emptyset$.
nodes.label: lem:regular_zero

nodes.statement: We say $G$ is \emph{locally bounded} if it is locally finite and there exists a constant $D$ such that, for all $x \in V(G)$, $\deg(x) \leq D$.
nodes.label: def:locally_bounded

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is \emph{bipartite} if there exists a partition $U_1$, $U_2$ of $V(G)$ such that, for all $e \in E(G)$, $e$ links an element of $U_1$ and an element of $U_2$.
nodes.label: def:bipartite

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. A \emph{dartwalk} from $x$ to $y$ on $G$ is given by a finite list $(d_1, \ldots, d_m)$ of darts, satisfying the following: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathrm{start}(d_1)=x$ and $\mathrm{end}(d_m)=y$; \item for any $i \in \{1, \ldots, m-1\}$, $\mathrm{end}(d_{i+1}) = \mathrm{start}(d_i)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:dartwalk

nodes.statement: The \emph{length} of a walk is its number of darts.
nodes.label: def:length

nodes.statement: The \emph{support} of the dartwalk $(d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ is the list $(x_i)_{0 \leq i \leq m}$ with $x_0=\mathrm{start}(d_1)$ and $x_i = \mathrm{end}(d_i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq m$.
nodes.label: def:dartwalk_support

nodes.statement: Let $w = (d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ be a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ and $w' = (d_i')_{1 \leq i \leq m'}$ be a dartwalk from $y$ to $z$. We define the \emph{concatenation} $w \cdot w'$ to be the dartwalk $(d_i'')_{1 \leq i \leq m+m'}$ where $d_i''=d_i$ for $i \leq m$ and $d_{i-m}'$ for $i > m$.
nodes.label: def:concatenation

nodes.statement: The length of the concatenation of two dartwalks is the sum of their lengths.
nodes.label: lem:length_concat

nodes.statement: We define a binary relation on $V(G)$ by: $x \sim y$ if there exists a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ on $G$. We then say $x$ and $y$ are \emph{reachable}.
nodes.label: def:reachable

nodes.statement: The reachability relation is an equivalence relation on $V(G)$.
nodes.label: prop:reachable_is_equivalence

nodes.statement: This is the same proof as in SimpleGraph.
Let $x$, $y$ in $V(G)$. If $x$ and $y$ are adjacent then $x$ and $y$ are reachable.
nodes.label: lem:adj_towalk

nodes.statement: A dartwalk $(d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ is called a \emph{path} if for all $1 \leq i,j \leq m$, $\mathrm{start}(d_i) = \mathrm{start}(d_j) \Rightarrow i=j$.
nodes.label: def:dartpath

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is a \emph{tree} if, for all $x$, $y \in V(G)$, there exists a unique path from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.label: def:tree

nodes.statement: A graph is \emph{preconnected} if any pair of vertices is reachable.
nodes.label: def:preconnected

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is \emph{connected} if it is preconnected and $V(G)$ is not empty.
nodes.label: def:connected

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is connected if and only if there exists $x \in V(G)$ such that, for all $y \in V(G)$, $x$ and $y$ are reachable.
nodes.label: lem:connected_iff_exists_forall_reachable

nodes.statement: A \emph{connected component} of $G$ is an equivalence class of $V(G)$ for the relation reachable.
nodes.label: def:connected_component

nodes.statement: For any vertex $x$, we define $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ to be the unique connected component of $G$ containing $x$.
nodes.label: def:connected_component_Mk

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. Then $\mathrm{cc}(x) = \mathrm{cc}(y)$ iff $x$ and $y$ are reachable.
nodes.label: lem:cc_eq

nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a connected component of $G$. Then the subgraph induced by $C$ is connected.
nodes.label: thm:cc_is_connected

nodes.statement: We denote as $\mathrm{ConnComp}(G)$ the set of connected components of $G$.
nodes.label: def:set_cc

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{ConnComp}(G)$ is a partition of $V(G)$.
nodes.label: prop:cc_is_partition

nodes.statement: If $V(G)$ is finite, then $\mathrm{ConnComp}(G)$ is finite and $\#V(G) \leq \# \mathrm{ConnComp}(G)$.
nodes.label: lem:bound_cc

nodes.statement: A \emph{function} $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a pair of functions $f_V : V(G_1) \rightarrow V(G_2)$ and $f_E : E(G_1) \rightarrow E(G_2)$. We will denote $f_V(x)=f(x)$ for $x \in V(G_1)$ and $f_E(e)=f(e)$ for $e \in E(G_1)$, i.e. view $f$ as a function from $V(G_1) \cup E(G_1)$ to $V(G_2) \cup E(G_2)$ sending vertices on vertices and edges on edges.
nodes.label: def:function_graphs

nodes.statement: A \emph{morphism} $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a function $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ such that for all $x, y \in V(G_1)$, $e \in E(G_1)$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $G_1$, then $f(e)$ links $f(x)$ and $f(y)$ in $G_2$.
nodes.label: def:graph_morphism

nodes.statement: A morphism $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is an \emph{isomorphism} if there exist a morphism $g : G_2 \rightarrow G_1$ which is the inverse of $f$. In this case we denote $f^{-1}$ this inverse.
nodes.label: def:graph_isomorphism

nodes.statement: A morphism $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a \emph{local isomorphism} if for all $x \in V(G_1)$, the restriction of $f$ to $\mathrm{incidenceSet}(x)$ is a bijection onto $\mathrm{incidenceSet}(f(x))$.
nodes.label: def:local_isomorphism

nodes.statement: A morphism $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a \emph{covering map} if it is surjective and a local isomorphism.
nodes.label: def:covering_map

nodes.statement: A graph $G_2$ is a \emph{covering graph} of a graph $G_1$ if there exists a covering map $\pi : G_2 \rightarrow G_1$.
nodes.label: def:covering_graph

nodes.statement: A \emph{rooted graph} is a graph $G$ with a distinguished vertex $r$, its \emph{root}.
nodes.label: def:rooted_graph

nodes.statement: Let $(G,r)$ be a rooted graph. Let $x \in V(G)$. A vertex $y \in V(G)$ is a \emph{parent} of $x$ if $y$ is adjacent to $x$ and $\mathrm{dist}(r,y) = \mathrm{dist}(r,x)-1$.
nodes.label: def:rooted_graph_parent

nodes.statement: Let $(G,r)$ be a rooted graph. A \emph{child} of $x \in V(G)$ is an adjacent vertice which is not a parent.
nodes.label: def:rooted_graph_child

nodes.statement: The root of a rooted graph has no parent.
nodes.label: lem:root_no_parent

nodes.statement: Let $(G,r)$ be a rooted graph. Assume $G$ is connected. Any vertex $x \in V(G)$ distinct from the root admits a parent.
nodes.label: lem:exists_parent

nodes.statement: A \emph{rooted tree} is a rooted graph $(G,r)$ which is a tree.
nodes.label: def:rooted_tree

nodes.statement: Let $(G,r)$ be a rooted tree. Any vertex $x \in V(G)$ distinct from the root admits a unique parent.
nodes.label: prop:rooted_tree_unique_parent

nodes.statement: A dartwalk $(d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ is called \emph{non-backtracking} if for all $1 \leq i < m$, $d_{i+1} \neq \mathrm{rev} (d_{i})$.
nodes.label: def:nonbacktracking

nodes.statement: Let $w = (d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ be a dartwalk. We say $w$ \emph{admits a reduction} if there exists $1 \leq j < m$ such that $d_{j+1} = \mathrm{rev}(d_j)$. In this case, we call the dartwalk $w'=(d_i')_{1 \leq i \leq m-2}$ obtained by letting $d_i'=d_i$ for $i<j$ and $d_i'=d_{i+2}$ for $i \geq j$ a \emph{reduction} of $w$.
nodes.label: def:walk_reduction

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. Two dartwalks $w = (d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ and $w' = (d_i')_{1 \leq i \leq m'}$ from $x$ to $y$ are said to be \emph{homotopic} if there exists a finite sequence $(w_j)_{1 \leq j \leq n}$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item for all $1 \leq j \leq n$, $w_j$ is a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$; \item $w_1=w$ and $w_n=w'$; \item for any $1 \leq j < n$, either $w_j$ is a reduction of $w_{j+1}$ or $w_{j+1}$ is a reduction of $w_j$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:homotopy

nodes.statement: The homotopy relation is an equivalence relation.
nodes.label: prop:homotopy_equivalence

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. Any dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ is homotopic to a unique nonbacktracking dartwalk, which we denote by $w_{\mathrm{nb}}$.
nodes.label: thm:unique_nonbacktracking

nodes.statement: Might be able to use the reduction results from coproduct library.

We define the \emph{universal cover} $\hat{G}$ of $(G,r)$, which is a rooted graph, by letting: \begin{itemize} \item $V(\hat G)$ be the set of non-backtracking dartwalks on $G$ starting at $r$; \item the dartset $D(\hat{G})$ is defined as the set of pairs $(w,d)$ where $w$ is a non-backtracking dartwalk ($w \in V(\hat{G})$) and $d \in D(G)$ is a dart on $G$ starting at the endpoint of $w$; \item for $(w,d) \in D(\hat{G})$, $\mathrm{start}_{\hat{G}}(w,d) = w$, $\mathrm{end}_{\hat{G}}(d) = (w \cdot d)_{\mathrm{nb}}$ and $\mathrm{rev}_{\hat{G}}(w,d) = ((w \cdot d)_{\mathrm{nb}},\mathrm{rev}_G(d))$; \item the root $\hat{r}$ is the empty walk from $r$ to $r$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:universal_cover

nodes.statement: The universal cover $(\hat{G}, \hat{r})$ of $(G,r)$ is a rooted tree.
nodes.label: thm:univ_cover_is_tree

nodes.statement: The projection map $\pi : \hat{G} \rightarrow G$ which is defined by $\pi(w)=\mathrm{end}(w)$ for $w \in V(\hat G)$ and $\pi(w,d)=d$ for $(w,d) \in D(\hat G)$ is a covering map.
nodes.label: thm:univ_cover_cover

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. The \emph{extended distance} $\mathrm{edist}(x,y)$ between $x$ and $y$ is the length of the shortest dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ (with value in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$).
nodes.label: def:edistance

nodes.statement: The \emph{distance} between $x$ and $y$ is $\mathrm{dist}(x,y) = \mathrm{edist}(x,y).\mathrm{toNat}$.
nodes.label: def:distance

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. $\mathrm{dist}(x,y) \neq 0$ iff $x \neq y$ and there exists a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.label: lem:distance_ne_zero

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$, we assume $\mathrm{dist}(x,y) \neq 0$. Then there exists a dartwalk of length $\mathrm{dist}(x,y)$ from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.label: lem:distance_take

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$ and $r \in \mathbb{N}$. We define the \emph{ball $B_r(x)$ of radius $r$ centered at $x$} as the set of vertices $y \in V(G)$ such that $\mathrm{edist}(x,y)\leq r$.
nodes.label: def:ball

nodes.statement: Assume $G$ is locally bounded and let $D = \sup_{x \in V(G)} \deg (x)$. Then, for any $x \in V(G)$, any $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $\# B_r(x) \leq D^r$.
nodes.label: prop:growth_ball

nodes.statement: todo
The \emph{extended diameter} of a graph $G$ is $\mathrm{ediam}(G) := \sup_{x,y \in V(G)} \mathrm{edist}(x,y)$.
nodes.label: def:ediameter

nodes.statement: The \emph{diameter} of $G$ is $\mathrm{diam}(G) = \mathrm{ediam}(G).\mathrm{toNat}$.
nodes.label: def:diameter

nodes.statement: Assume $V(G)$ is finite and non-empty. Then $\mathrm{diam}(G) \neq 0$ if and only if $G$ is connected.
nodes.label: lem:connected_iff_diam_ne_zero

nodes.statement: To be adapted from SimpleGraph.
Assume $G$ is a graph of finite diameter. For any $x \in V(G)$, $V(G)$ is included in the ball of radius $\mathrm{diam}(G)$ centered at $x$.
nodes.label: lem:vertexset_incl_ball_diam

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. By definition of the diameter, $\mathrm{dist}(x,y) \leq \mathrm{diam}(G)$ and hence $y$ lies in the ball of radius $\mathrm{diam}(G)$ centered at $x$.
Let $G$ be a regular graph of degree $\mathfrak{d}$. Assume $V(G)$ is finite and not empty. Then \begin{equation} \mathrm{diam}(G) \geq \log_{\mathfrak{d}} \# V(G). \end{equation}
nodes.label: prop:bound_diameter_regular

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:vertexset_incl_ball_diam}, if $r := \mathrm{diam}(G)$, then $V(G) \subseteq B_r(x)$. In particular $\# V(G) \leq \# B_r(X) \leq \mathfrak{d}^r$ by Proposition \ref{prop:growth_ball}.
A function $V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is \emph{constant} if, for all $x, y \in V(G)$, $f(x)=f(y)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: def:constant_function

nodes.statement: The constant function equal to $1$ is defined by \begin{equation} \mathbf{1} : \begin{cases} V(G) & \rightarrow \mathbb{C} \\ x & \mapsto 1. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: def:constant_one

nodes.statement: Assume $V(G)$ is not empty. Then $\mathbf{1} \neq 0$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:one_neq_zero

nodes.statement: If $V(G)$ is not empty, then there exists $x \in V(G)$. Then $\mathbf{1} (x) = 1 \neq 0$, and hence $\mathbf{1} \neq 0$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: Assume $V(G)$ is not empty. Then the space of constant functions is a vectorial subspace of $\mathbb{C}^{V(G)}$, of dimension $1$, generated by $\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: thm:space_constant

nodes.statement: We directly check that: \begin{itemize} \item the constant function equal to $0$ is constant; \item for any constant functions $f_1$, $f_2$ and any $c \in \mathbb{C}$, the function $f_1+cf_2$ is also constant; \end{itemize} both by direct application of the definition. We also check that the function $\mathbf{1}$ is constant. Let $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a constant function. Since $V(G)$ is not empty there exists $x \in V(G)$. Then for all $y \in V(G), f(y) = f(x) \mathbf{1}(y)$, so $f = f(x) \mathbf{1}$, which allows to conclude.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: The space of constant functions is included in $\ell^2(G)$ if and only if $V(G)$ is finite.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:constant_is_l2

nodes.statement: Assume $V(G)$ is non-empty and finite. Then, the orthogonal of the space of constant functions is \begin{equation*} \mathbf{1}^\perp = \Big\{ f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C} : \sum_{x \in V(G)}f(x)=0 \Big\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:orth_constant

nodes.statement: By definition of the orthogonal, $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ is the space of functions $f \in \ell^2(G)$ such that $\langle f, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$. Since $V(G)$ is finite all functions $V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ are in $\ell^2(G)$. By definition of the scalar product and the constant function, $\langle f, \mathbf{1} \rangle = \sum_{x \in V(G)}f(x)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a subset of $V(G)$. We define the \emph{indicator function} $\mathbf{1}_U : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ by \begin{equation} \mathbf{1}_U (x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \in U \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: def:indicator_function

nodes.statement: The indicator function of a set $U$ is in $\ell^2(G)$ iff $U$ is finite.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:indicator_ell2

nodes.statement: Let $(\pi_U)_{U \in I}$ be a partition of $V(G)$. Then $\mathbf{1} = \sum_{U \in I} \mathbf{1}_U$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:partition_unity

nodes.statement: A function $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is said to be \emph{locally constant} if, for all $x,y \in V(G)$, if $x$ is adjacent to $y$, then $f(x)=f(y)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: def:locally_constant

nodes.statement: Let $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $f$ is locally constant; \item for every $x \in V(G)$, for every $d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)$, $f(x)=f(\mathrm{end}(d))$. \item for every $d \in D(G)$, $f(\mathrm{start}(d))=f(\mathrm{end}(d))$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:dart_locally_constant

nodes.statement: Let $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a locally constant function. For any $x, y \in V(G)$, if $x$ and $y$ are reachable, then $f(x)=f(y)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:locally_constant_walk

nodes.statement: By induction.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: A locally constant function on a preconnected graph is constant.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:locally_constant_preconnected

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a preconnected graph and $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a locally constant function. For any $x$, $y$ in $V(G)$, by Definition \ref{def:preconnected}, there exists a walk from $x$ to $y$. Lemma \ref{lem:locally_constant_walk} this implies $f(x)=f(y)$. Hence by Definition \ref{def:constant_function}, $f$ is constant.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: The restriction of a locally constant function to a subgraph is locally constant on that subgraph.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:locally_constant_subgraph

nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a locally constant function on $G$, and $H$ be a subgraph of $G$. Let $x, y$ be adjacent vertices in $H$. By Lemma \ref{lem:subgraph_adj_graph}, $x$ and $y$ are also adjacent in $G$. Then $f(x)=f(y)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: A function $f$ is locally constant if and only if its restriction to each connected component is a constant function.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: thm:locally_constant_cc

nodes.statement: Assume $f$ is locally constant. Let $C$ be a connected component of $G$. By Lemma \ref{lem:locally_constant_subgraph}, the restriction of $f$ to $C$ is locally constant. By Theorem \ref{thm:cc_is_connected}, $C$ is preconnected. So by Lemma \ref{lem:locally_constant_preconnected}, the restriction of $f$ to $C$ is constant. Assume the restriction of $f$ to each connected component is constant. Let $x$, $y$ be adjacent vertices. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:cc_eq}, $\mathrm{cc}(x) = \mathrm{cc}(y)$ which implies that $y \in \mathrm{cc}(x)$. This allows to conclude since $f$ is constant on $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ by hypothesis and Theorem \ref{thm:cc_is_connected}.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: The indicator function of a connected component is locally constant.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: lem:indicator_cc_loc_const

nodes.statement: The space of locally constant functions is a vectorial subspace of the space of functions $V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, and the $\{\mathbf{1}_C, C \in \mathrm{ConnComp}(G)\}$ are a basis of this space.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: thm:locally_constant_basis

nodes.statement: We directly check that: \begin{itemize} \item the constant function equal to $0$ is locally constant; \item for any locally constant functions $f_1$, $f_2$ and any $c \in \mathbb{C}$, the function $f_1+cf_2$ is also locally constant; \end{itemize} both by direct application of the definition. Now, for any connected component $C$, $\mathbf{1}_C$ is locally constant by Lemma \ref{lem:indicator_cc_loc_const}. We prove these functions form a basis using the fact that, by Proposition \ref{prop:cc_is_partition} and Lemma \ref{lem:partition_unity}, \begin{equation*} \mathbf{1} = \sum_{C \in \mathrm{ConnComp}(G)} \mathbf{1}_C \end{equation*} and hence if $f$ is locally constant, \begin{equation*} \forall x \in V(G), f(x) = \sum_{C \in \mathrm{ConnComp}(G)} f(x) \mathbf{1}_C(x). \end{equation*} The function $f$ is constant on each connected component so this is a decomposition in the desired basis. The decomposition is unique as for all $x \in V(G)$, the coefficient associated to $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ must be $f(x)$ since $\mathbf{1}_C(x)=0$ for all other connected component.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph

nodes.statement: The dimension of the space of locally constant functions is the number of connected components of $G$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Space of functions on a graph
nodes.label: cor:dimension_locally_constant

nodes.statement: We define the adjacency operator $a$ as the linear operator acting on the space of functions $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ by $$ a f (x) := \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(d)} f(\mathrm{end}(x)).$$
nodes.label: def:adjacency_operator

nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a locally constant function. Then, for all $x \in V(G)$, $af(x) = \deg(x) f(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:adjacency_locally_constant

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. By definition, \begin{equation*} af(x) = \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)). \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{lem:adjacent_vs_dart}, for all $d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)$, $\mathrm{end}(d)$ is adjacent to $x$ and in particular $f(\mathrm{end}(d))=f(x)$. This leads to the conclusion by Definition \ref{def:degree}.
For any $x \in V(G)$, $a \mathbf{1}(x) = \deg(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:adjacency_of_constant

nodes.statement: Assume $G$ is locally bounded. Then the adjacency operator is a bounded operator on $\ell^2(G)$ and its norm satisfies $\|a\| \leq \sup_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x)$.
nodes.label: thm:norm_adjacency_leq_sup_degree

nodes.statement: For any function $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, any vertex $x \in V(G)$, \begin{equation} |af(x)|^2 \leq \deg(x) \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} |f(\mathrm{end}(d))|^2. \end{equation} Furthermore, this is an equality if and only if for any $y, z$ adjacent to $x$, $f(y) = f(z)$.
nodes.label: lem:bound_a_degree_x

nodes.statement: Let $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and $x \in V(G)$. By Definition \ref{def:adjacency_operator}, \begin{equation} |af(x)|^2 = \Big| \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d))\Big|^2. \end{equation} By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the complex vectors $v_1 := (1)_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)}$ and $v_2 := (f(\mathrm{end}(d)))_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)}$ we have \begin{align*} |af(x)|^2 & = \left| v_1 \cdot v_2 \right|^2 \leq \|v_1\|_2^2 \|v_2\|_2^2 \\ &\leq \left( \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} 1 \right) \left( \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} |f(\mathrm{end}(d))|^2 \right). \end{align*} This leads to the inequality by Definition \ref{def:degree}. The equality case comes from the equality case in Cauchy-Schwarz, which occurs if and only if the vectors $v_1$ and $v_2$ are colinear, which is equivalent to the announced condition as $v_1$ is a non-zero constant vector, using Lemma \ref{lem:adjacent_vs_dart}.

Assume $G$ is locally bounded. Then, for any $f \in \ell^2(G)$, $a f \in \ell^2(G)$ and \begin{equation} \|a f\| \leq \sup_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x) \times \|f\|. \end{equation} Furthermore, the equality occurs if and only if $G$ is regular of degree $\delta$ for some non-negative integer $\delta$ and, for any $x \in V(G)$, for any $y$ and $z$ adjacent to $x$, $f(y)=f(z)$.
nodes.label: lem:bound_a_sup_degree

nodes.statement: Let us write $D := \sup_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x)$. By definition, \begin{equation*} \|af\|^2 = \sum_{x \in V(G)} |af(x)|^2 \end{equation*} and $af \in \ell^2(G)$ iff this sum is finite. We sum Lemma \ref{lem:bound_a_degree_x} for all vertices of $G$ and obtain that \begin{equation*} \_ \leq \sum_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x) \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} |f(\mathrm{end}(d))|^2 \leq D \sum_{d \in D(G)} |f(\mathrm{end}(d))|^2. \end{equation*} We apply the involution $\mathrm{rev}$ to the sum, changing indices, to obtain \begin{equation*} \_ = D \sum_{d \in D(G)} |f(\mathrm{end}(\mathrm{rev}(d)))|^2 = D \sum_{d \in D(G)} |f(\mathrm{start}(d))|^2. \end{equation*} Now by Definitions \ref{def:dartset} and \ref{def:degree} \begin{equation*} \_ = D \sum_{x \in V(G)} \sum_{x \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} |f(\mathrm{start}(d))|^2 = D \sum_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x) |f(x)|^2 \leq D^2 \sum_{x \in V(G)} |f(x)|^2 = D^2 \|f\|^2. \end{equation*} This means that $af \in \ell^2(G)$ and $\|af\| \leq D \|f\|$, which was our claim. If the equality occurs, since all terms are non-negative, it means that $\deg (x)$ is constant (i.e. the graph is regular), and that there is equality in each term of Lemma \ref{lem:bound_a_degree_x}, which is the conclusion.
The adjacency operator is selfadjoint.
nodes.label: prop:adjacency_is_selfadjoint

nodes.statement: For any $f$, $g$ in $\ell^2(G)$, \begin{equation} \langle af, g \rangle = \sum_{d \in D(G)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)) \overline{g(\mathrm{start}(d))}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:scalar_of_adjacency

nodes.statement: Let $f$, $g$ be elements of $\ell^2(G)$. By Proposition \ref{lem:bound_a_sup_degree}, $a f \in \ell^2(G)$. By definition of the scalar product, \begin{equation} \langle af, g \rangle = \sum_{x \in V(G)} af(x) \overline{g(x)}. \end{equation} By Definition \ref{def:adjacency_operator}, \begin{equation} \langle af, g \rangle = \sum_{x \in V(G)} \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)) \overline{g(x)} \end{equation} which we can rewrite as the claim.

Let $f$, $g$ be elements of $\ell^2(G)$. We have by Lemma \ref{lem:scalar_of_adjacency} \begin{equation*} \langle af, g \rangle = \sum_{d \in D(G)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)) \overline{g(\mathrm{start}(d))} = \overline{\sum_{d \in D(G)} g(\mathrm{end}(d)) \overline{f(\mathrm{start}(d))}} \end{equation*} by complex conjugation and applying the involution $\mathrm{rev}$ to exchange the start and end of each dart. Hence by Lemma \ref{lem:scalar_of_adjacency} \begin{equation*} \langle af, g \rangle = \overline{\langle ag, f \rangle} = \langle f, ag \rangle. \end{equation*} This means that $a^*=a$ by definition of the adjoint, which means $a$ is self-adjoint by definition.
The spectrum of the adjacency operator is real.
nodes.label: cor:spectrum_is_real

nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{prop:adjacency_is_selfadjoint} with selfAdjoint.mem\_spectrum\_eq\_re.
The spectrum of $a$ is included in the segment $[-D,D]$ where $D = \sup_{x \in V(G)} \deg(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:spectrum_in_segment

nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{cor:spectrum_is_real}, the spectrum of $a$ is real. By spectrum.subset\_closedBall\_norm, it is included in the closed ball of center $0$ and radius $\|a\|$. We have $\|a\| \leq D$ by Theorem \ref{thm:norm_adjacency_leq_sup_degree}.
If $V(G)$ is finite, then the spectrum of the adjacency operator is a family of $\# V(G)$ eigenvalues.
nodes.label: lem:spectrum_finite

nodes.statement: If $V(G)$ is finite, then $\ell^2(G)$ has finite dimension. So this is just the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators in finite dimension.
Let $x, y \in V(G)$. Then \begin{equation*} \langle a \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}, \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}} \rangle = \# \mathrm{dartSet}(x,y). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:coefficients_adjacency_expression

nodes.statement: The functions $\mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}$ and $\mathbf{1}_{\{y\}}$ are trivially in $\ell^2(G)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:scalar_of_adjacency}, \begin{equation*} \langle a \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}, \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}} \rangle = \sum_{d \in D(G)} \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}(\mathrm{start}(d)) \overline{\mathbf{1}_{\{y\}}(\mathrm{end}(d))} \end{equation*} which is exactly the claim by Definition \ref{def:dartset_pair} and Definition \ref{def:indicator_function}.
For any $x, y \in V(G)$, $\langle a \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}, \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}} \rangle$ is a non-negative integer, which is even as soon as $x=y$.
nodes.label: lem:coefficients_adjacency_properties

nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:coefficients_adjacency_expression}, this quantity is a cardinal of a set, and hence a non-negative integer. The parity when $x=y$ comes from Lemma \ref{lem:darset_loop_even}.

Let $V$ be a set. An operator $a : V^{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow V^{\mathbb{C}}$ is \emph{adjacency-like} if it satisfies the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item for all $x \in V$, $a \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}} \in \ell^2(G)$; \item for all $x, y \in V$, $a_{x,y} := \langle a \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}, \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}} \rangle$ is a non-negative integer; \item for all $x, y \in V$, $a_{x,y}=a_{y,x}$; \item for all $x \in V$, $a_{x,x}$ is even. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:adjacency_like

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set and $a$ be an adjacency-like operator on $V$. We define a dart-like structure on $V$ by taking: \begin{itemize} \item $D$ is the set of $(x,y,i)$ where $x \in V$, $y \in V$, and $i$ is an integer such that \begin{itemize} \item if $x \neq y$ then $1 \leq i \leq a_{x,y}$; \item if $x=y$ then $1 \leq |i| \leq a_{x,x}$. \end{itemize} \item for any $(x,y,i) \in D$, we let $\mathrm{start}(x,y,i)=x$, $\mathrm{end}(x,y,i)=y$ and \begin{equation*} \mathrm{rev}(x,y,i) := \begin{cases} \mathrm{rev}(y,x,i) & \text{if } x \neq y \\ \mathrm{rev}(x,y,-i) & \text{if } x = y. \end{cases} \end{equation*} \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:dartlike_of_adjlike

nodes.statement: Let $a$ be a adjacency-like operator on $V$. We define the graph associated to $a$ by taking the graph associated to the dartlike structure associated to $a$.
nodes.label: def:graph_of_adjlike

nodes.statement: Let $a$ be a adjacency-like operator on $V$. Then the graph $G$ associated to $a$ is a graph, of vertex set $V$, and adjacency operator $a$.
nodes.label: lem:adjacency_of_graph_of_adjacency

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set. The space of adjacency-like operators on $V$ is stable by addition, i.e. if $a$, $a'$ are adjacency-like, so is $a+a'$.
nodes.label: lem:adjlike_addition

nodes.statement: Assume $G$ is not empty and locally finite. Then $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ iff $a \mathbf{1} = \mathfrak{d} \mathbf{1}$.
nodes.label: lem:adjacency_of_constant_regular

nodes.statement: By Definition \ref{def:regular}, $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ if and only if for all $x \in V(G)$, $\deg(x)=\mathfrak{d}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:adjacency_of_constant}, this is equivalent to having, for all $x \in V(G)$, $a \mathbf{1} (x) = \mathfrak{d}$, which is equivalent to $a \mathbf{1} = \mathfrak{d} \mathbf{1}$ by Definition \ref{def:constant_one}.
Assume $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then $\mathfrak{d}$ is an eigenvalue of the adjacency operator with associated eigenfunction the constant function $\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.label: lem:constant_eigenfunction_regular

nodes.statement: Since $G$ is finite, $\mathbf{1} \in \ell^2(G)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:constant_is_l2}. Furthermore, $\mathbf{1} \neq 0$ by Lemma \ref{lem:one_neq_zero}. By Lemma \ref{lem:adjacency_of_constant_regular}, if $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$, then $a \mathbf{1} = \mathfrak{d} \mathbf{1}$. We conclude by the definition of eigenvalue and eigenvector.
If $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite, then $\|a\|=\mathfrak{d}$.
nodes.label: prop:norm_adjacency_regular

nodes.statement: Since $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$, by Theorem \ref{thm:norm_adjacency_leq_sup_degree}, $\|a \| \leq \mathfrak{d}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:constant_eigenfunction_regular}, $\mathfrak{d}$ is an eigenvalue of $a$ and hence $\|a\| \geq \mathfrak{d}$, which is enough to conclude.
Assume $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\mathfrak{d}$ is exactly the number of connected components of $G$.
nodes.label: prop:regular_multiplicity_trivial_eigenvalue

nodes.statement: We treat differently the case $\mathfrak{d}=0$, where $a$ is identically equal to $0$ and every function $V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is in the kernel of $a$, and hence the result holds since the connected components of $G$ are all the $\{x\}$ for $x \in V(G)$. Now assume $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$. Lemma \ref{lem:adjacency_locally_constant} implies that all locally constant functions are included in the eigenspace associated to the eigenvalue $\mathfrak{d}$. Let us show the other inclusion. Assume $f$ is such that $af=\mathfrak{d} f$. In particular, $\|af\|=\mathfrak{d}\|f\|$ and hence by the equality case in Lemma \ref{lem:bound_a_sup_degree}, \begin{equation*} \forall x \in V(G), \forall y, z \text{ adjacent to } x, f(y)=f(z). \end{equation*} In particular \begin{equation*} \mathfrak{d} f(x) = af(x) = \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)). \end{equation*} Note that this sum contains $\mathfrak{d}$ terms and, for all $d,d' \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)$, $f(\mathrm{end}(d))=f(\mathrm{end}(d'))$ so all of its terms are equal. Since $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$, we obtain that, for all $d, d' \in \mathrm{dartSet}(G)$, $f(\mathrm{end}(d))=f(\mathrm{end}(d'))$, i.e. $f$ is locally constant. By Theorem \ref{thm:locally_constant_basis}, the dimension of the space of locally constant functions is exactly the number of connected components of $G$, which allows to conclude.
Assume $G$ regular of degree $\mathfrak{d} \geq 1$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then $-\mathfrak{d}$ is an eigenvalue of $a$ if and only if $G$ has a bipartite connected component.
nodes.label: prop:eigenvalue_regular_bipartite

nodes.statement: Assume $G$ is preconnected and $E(G)$ is non-empty. Then $G$ is bipartite iff there exists a non-zero function $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that, for all $x, y \in V(G)$, if $x$ and $y$ are adjacent, then $f(x)=-f(y)$.
nodes.label: lem:bipartite_odd_function

nodes.statement:

For any $x, y \in V(G)$ adjacent, one of the following occurs:  egin{itemize} \item either $x \in U_1$ and $y \in U_2$, and hence $f(x)=1=-f(y)$; \item or $x \in U_2$ and $y \in U_1$, and hence $f(x)=-1=-f(y)$. \end{itemize} Now assume there exists a non-zero function $f : V(G) ightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that, for any $x, y \in V(G)$ adjacent, $f(x)=-f(y)$. By assumption, $E(G)$ is not empty, so there exists $x \in V(G)$ with at least an adjacent vertex. For any $y \in V(G)$, since $G$ is preconnected, there exists a walk $w$ from $x$ to $y$. We check by induction that the hypothesis on $f$ implies $f(y) = (-1)^{\mathrm{length}(w)}f(x)$. Since $f

eq 0$, $U_1 \cap U_2 = \emptyset$. \item $U_1$ contains $x$ and is hence not empty. We picked $x$ so that it has at least one adjacent edge, which will be an element of $U_2$, and hence $U_2$ is not empty. \item For any edge $e \in E(G)$ linking two vertices $y, z$, we check that $y \in U_1 \Rightarrow x \in U_2$ and $y \in U_2 \Rightarrow z \in U_1$ thanks to the fact that $f(y)=-f(z)$. \end{itemize} So, $G$ is bipartite.

Let us assume that $- \mathfrak{d}$ is an eigenvalue of $a$. Then by definition there exists a non-zero function $f \in \ell^2(G)$ such that $af=-\mathfrak{d} f$. In particular $\|af\|=\mathfrak{d} \|f\|$. By the equality case in Lemma ef{lem:bound_a_sup_degree}, for any $x \in V(G)$, any $y, z$ adjacent to $x$, $f(y)=f(z)$. But then we have for $x \in V(G)$  egin{equation*} - \mathfrak{d} f(x) = af(x) = \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)) \end{equation*} a sum with $\mathfrak{d} 
eq 0$ terms in which all terms are equal. Hence for any $y$ adjacent to $x$, $f(y)=-f(x)$. Since $f 
eq 0$, there exists $x \in V(G)$ such that $f(x) 
eq 0$. We apply Lemma ef{lem:bipartite_odd_function} to the graph $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ with the restriction of the function $f$ (which we can do as $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ is preconnected and has at least one edge since $\deg(x) = \mathfrak{d} \geq 1$), and obtain that $\mathrm{cc}(x)$ is bipartite. Now, let us assume that one connected component $C$ of $G$ is bipartite. $C$ is not empty so it contains at least one vertex, which has at least one incident edge as the graph is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d} \geq 1$. Hence we can apply Lemma ef{lem:bipartite_odd_function} to $C$ and obtain a function $f$ such that, for any $x$, $y$ adjacent, $f(x)=-f(y)$. Then, let us define $F(x) = f(x)$ if $x \in C$ and $0$ otherwise. $F \in \ell^2(G)$ since $G$ is finite. We check that $aF=- \mathfrak{d} F$ (here using the fact that, if $x$, $y$ are adjacent, then $x \in C \Leftrightarrow y \in C$). $F 
eq 0$ as there exists $x \in C \subset V(G)$ for which $F(x) = f(x)

Assume $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then the operator $a$ induces a bounded self-adjoint operator $a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}$ on the orthogonal of $\mathbf{1}$ in $\ell^2(G)$, and $\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| \leq d$.
nodes.label: lem:projection_orth_constant

nodes.statement: This is classic theory of self-adjoint bounded operators, as $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of $a$ by Lemma \ref{lem:constant_eigenfunction_regular}.

Assume $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then there exists $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and a non-zero function $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $af=\lambda f$, $\sum_{x \in V(G)}f(x)=0$ and $|\lambda| = \|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\|$.
nodes.label: lem:norm_perp_is_eig

nodes.statement: The operator $a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}$ is a self-adjoint operator in finite dimension by Lemma \ref{lem:projection_orth_constant}, and hence its spectrum is entirely made of real eigenvalues and its norm is the supremum of their absolute values. Hence there exists a function $f \in \mathbf{1}^\perp$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}f = \lambda f$, $f \neq 0$ and $|\lambda|=\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\|$. The function $f$ and the number $\lambda$ satisfy the claim.
Assume $G$ is regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ and $V(G)$ is finite. Then, $\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| = \mathfrak{d}$ iff $G$ is disconnected or bipartite.
nodes.label: prop:gap_iff

nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:norm_perp_is_eig}, there exists a function $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and a real number $\lambda$ such that $af=\lambda f$, $|\lambda|=\mathfrak{d}$ and $\sum_{x \in V(G)} f(x)=0$. Since $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, either $\lambda = \mathfrak{d}$ or $\lambda=-\mathfrak{d}$. \begin{itemize} \item If $\lambda = \mathfrak{d}$, then since $f$ is not constant (otherwise it would be equal to $0$ as $\sum_{x \in V(G)}f(x)=0$), the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\mathfrak{d}$ for $a$ is at least $2$. By Proposition \ref{prop:regular_multiplicity_trivial_eigenvalue}, the number of connected components of $G$ is $\geq 2$ and hence $G$ is disconnected. \item If $\lambda = -\mathfrak{d}$, then $-\mathfrak{d}$ is an eigenvalue of $a$. By Proposition \ref{prop:eigenvalue_regular_bipartite}, $G$ has a connected component $C$ that is bipartite. \begin{itemize} \item If $C=V(G)$ then $G$ is bipartite. \item Otherwise $G$ is disconnected as it has a strict connected component. \end{itemize} \end{itemize}

Let $G$ be a regular graph of degree $\mathfrak{d}$ with a finite diameter. Then, \begin{equation*} \|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| \geq 2 \sqrt{2 \mathfrak{d} -1} - \frac{2 \sqrt{2 \mathfrak{d} -1}-1}{\lfloor \mathrm{diam} (G) /2 \rfloor}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: thm:Alon_Boppana

nodes.statement: A graph $G$ is a $\mathfrak{d}$-regular tree if it is a tree and regular of degree $\mathfrak{d}$.
nodes.label: def:regular_tree

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a $\mathfrak{d}$-regular tree. Then $\|a\| = 2 \sqrt{\mathfrak{d}-1}$.
nodes.label: thm:regular_tree_norm

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 2$ be a integer and $\mathfrak{d} = 2r$. For any $\epsilon > 0$, \begin{equation} \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| \leq 2 \sqrt{2\mathfrak{d} -1} + \epsilon) = 1. \end{equation}
nodes.label: thm:Friedman

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 2$ be an integer and $\mathfrak{d} = 2r$. Then, \begin{equation} \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(G_{\vec{\pi}} \text{ is connected})=1 \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(G_{\vec{\pi}} \text{ is bipartite})=0. \end{equation}
nodes.label: prop:random_connected_non_bipartite

nodes.statement: Denote $A = "G_{\vec{\pi}} \text{ is disconnected}"$ and $B = "G_{\vec{\pi}} \text{ is bipartite}"$. By Proposition \ref{prop:gap_iff}, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(A \cup B) = \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| = 2r). \end{equation*} We check directly that $2 \sqrt{2 \mathfrak{d} - 1} < \mathfrak{d}$. Hence taking $\epsilon = (\mathfrak{d} - 2 \sqrt{2 \mathfrak{d} - 1})/2 > 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} \forall x, \quad x = \mathfrak{d} \Rightarrow x > 2 \sqrt{2\mathfrak{d} -1} + \epsilon. \end{equation*} Hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(A \cup B) \leq \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(\|a|_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}\| > 2 \sqrt{2\mathfrak{d} -1} + \epsilon) \end{equation*} which goes to $0$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$ by Theorem \ref{thm:Friedman}. So $\lim_N \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(A) = 0$ and $\lim_N \mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}(B)=0$ which allows to conclude.

Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer. To a family $\vec{\pi} = (\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_r) \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}^r$ we associate a dart-like structure on $V$ by taking: \begin{itemize} \item $D = V \times \{1, \ldots, r\} \times \{-1,+1\}$ \item for $(x,i,\epsilon) \in D$, we let $\mathrm{start}(x,i,\epsilon) = x$, $\mathrm{end}(x,i,\epsilon) = \pi_i^\epsilon(x)$ and $\mathrm{rev}(x,i,\epsilon) = (\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:dart_of_pi

nodes.statement: We check that \begin{equation*} \mathrm{start}(\mathrm{rev}(x,i,\epsilon)) = \mathrm{start}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon) = \pi_i^\epsilon(x) = \mathrm{end}(x,i,\epsilon) \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \mathrm{end}(\mathrm{rev}(x,i,\epsilon)) = \mathrm{end}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon) = \pi_i^{-\epsilon}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x)) = x = \mathrm{start}(x,i,\epsilon) \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \mathrm{rev}(\mathrm{rev}(x,i,\epsilon)) = \mathrm{rev}((\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon)) = (\pi_i^{-\epsilon}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x)),i,--\epsilon) = (x,i,\epsilon). \end{equation*}

Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer. To a family $\vec{\pi} \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}^r$ we associate a graph $G_{\vec{\pi}}$ on $V$ by taring the graph associated to the dart-like structure associated to $\vec{\pi}$.
nodes.label: def:graph_of_pi

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer and take $\vec{\pi} = (\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_r) \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}^r$. Then, for any $x, y \in V$, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{dartSet}(x,y) = \{(x,i,\epsilon): y = \pi_i^\epsilon(x)\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:dartset_pair_pi

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer and take $\vec{\pi} = (\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_r) \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}^r$. Then, for any $x \in V$, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{dartSet}(x) = \{(x,i,\epsilon): 1 \leq i \leq r, \epsilon = \pm 1\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:dartset_pi

nodes.statement: The graph $G_{\vec{\pi}}$ is regular of degree $2r$.
nodes.label: lem:graph_pi_regular

nodes.statement: For $\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}$, we define an operator $u_\pi : V^{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow V^{\mathbb{C}}$ by letting, for $f : V \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, \begin{equation*} \forall x \in V, u_\pi f(x) = f(\pi^{-1}(x)) \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:u_pi

nodes.statement: For $\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}$, the operator $u_\pi$ is a unitary operator on $\ell^2(V)$ and $u_\pi^*=u_\pi^{-1}=u_{\pi^{-1}}$.
nodes.label: lem:u_pi_unitary

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer. For any family $\vec{\pi} = (\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_r) \in \mathfrak{S}_{V}^r$, the adjacency operator $a_{\vec{\pi}}$ of $G_{\vec{\pi}}$ can be written as \begin{equation*} a_{\vec{\pi}} = \sum_{i=1}^r (u_{\pi_i} + u_{\pi_i}^*). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:adjacency_of_pi

nodes.statement: We have by definition of the adjacency operator for a function $f : V \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and $x \in V$, \begin{equation*} af(x) = \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dartSet}(x)} f(\mathrm{end}(d)) = \sum_{i=1}^r \sum_{\epsilon = \pm 1} f(\pi_i^\epsilon(x)) = \sum_{i=1}^r (f(\pi_i^{-1}(x)) + f(\pi_i(x))) \end{equation*} which leads to the conclusion as we recognise $u_{\pi_i}$ and $u_{\pi_i^{-1}} = u_{\pi_i}^*$.
We equip $\mathfrak{S}_{N}^r$ with the uniform probability measure which we denote as $\mathrm{Prob}_{N,r}$. We denote the corresponding expectation by $\mathbb{E}_{N,r}$.
nodes.label: def:probability_measure

nodes.statement: For any function $F : \mathfrak{S}_{N}^r \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, \begin{equation*} \mathbb{E}_{N,r} [F(\vec{\pi})] = \frac{1}{N!^r} \sum_{\vec{\pi} \in \mathfrak{S}_{N}^r} F(\vec{\pi}). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:formula_expec

nodes.statement: This is the expectation for a uniform measure, noting that the cardinal of $\mathfrak{S}_{N}$ is $N!^r$.

Denote $\mathfrak{d} = 2r$. Let $\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{d},N}$ be the set of $\mathfrak{d}$-regular graphs with $V(G) = [N]$, equiped with the power-set $\sigma$-algebra. We define a probability measure $\mathrm{Prob}_{N,\mathfrak{d}}^{G}$ on $\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{d},N}$ by pushing forward $\mathrm{Prob}_{N,r}$ with the function $\mathfrak{S}_{N}^r \rightarrow \mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{d},N}$ defined in Definition \ref{def:graph_of_pi}.
nodes.label: def:proba_on_graphs

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group with neutral element $\mathbf{1}$. To a family $(x_1, \ldots, x_r) \in G^r$ we associate a family $(x_0, \ldots, x_{2r}) \in G^{2r+1}$ by letting $x_0= \mathbf{1}$ and for $1 \leq i \leq r$, $x_{r+i} := x_i^{-1}$.
nodes.label: def:numbering_convention

nodes.statement: We denote as $\mathbf{W}_r$ the set of finite words $w = w_1 \ldots w_q$ in the letters $\{0, \ldots 2r\}$. The \emph{length} $|w| = q$ of a word $w$ is its number of letters.
nodes.label: def:word

nodes.statement: Let $w = w_1 \ldots w_q \in \mathbf{W}_r$ and $G$ be a group with neutral element $\mathbf{1}$. The \emph{word map} $w : G^r \rightarrow G$ is defined by letting, for each $(x_1, \ldots, x_r) \in G^r$, $w(x_1, \ldots, x_r) = x_{w_1} \ldots x_{w_q}$ with the numbering convention from Definition \ref{def:numbering_convention}.
nodes.label: def:word_map

nodes.statement: The \emph{normalised trace} $\mathrm{tr}_{N} : \mathcal{M}_N(\mathbb{C}) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is defined by $\mathrm{tr}_{N} := \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{Tr}_{N}$.
nodes.label: def:normalised_trace

nodes.statement: Let $q \geq 1$ be an integer. For $1 \leq j \leq q-1$, we define $r_{r,q,j} := \min (r, \lfloor q/(j+1) \rfloor)$ and we define the polynomial $g_{r,q}(x) = \prod_{j=1}^{q-1} (1-j x)^{r_{r,q,j}}$.
nodes.label: def:gq

nodes.statement: For any $q \geq 1$, the degree of $g_{r,q}$ is at most $q(1+\log r)-1$.
nodes.label: lem:degree_gq

nodes.statement: By comparaison with an integral, we have \begin{align*} \deg g_{r,q} = \sum_{j=1}^{q-1} r_{r,q,j} \leq \int_1^q \min(r, q/x) \, \mathrm{d} x \leq q(1+\log r) - \min(r,q). \end{align*}

Let $q \geq 1$. Let $w \in \mathbf{W}_r$ be a word of length at most $q$. There exists a polynomial $f_w$, of degree at most $q(1+\log r)$, such that for any $N \geq q$, \begin{equation*} \mathbb{E}_{N,r} [\mathrm{tr}_{N} w(\vec \pi)] = \frac{f_w(1/N)}{g_q(1/N)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: thm:expectation_word_formula

nodes.statement: Let $D \geq 1$ and $r \geq 1$. A \emph{non-commutative polynomial with matrix coefficients} $P \in \mathcal{M}_D(\mathbb{C}) \otimes \mathbb{C} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_{r} \rangle$ is an expression of the form $\sum_{w \in \mathbf{W}_r} A_w \otimes w(x_1, \ldots, x_{r})$.
nodes.label: def:non_comm_poly

nodes.statement: Let $P = \sum_{w \in \mathbf{W}_r} A_w \otimes w(x_1, \ldots, x_{r})\in \mathcal{M}_D(\mathbb{C}) \otimes \mathbb{C} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_{r} \rangle$. For $(U_1, \ldots, U_r)$ be a $r$-tuple of unitary matrices of shared dimension, we define $P(U_1, \ldots, U_r) = \sum_{w \in \mathbf{W}_r} A_w \otimes w(U_1, \ldots, U_r)$ using the word map defined in Definition \ref{def:word_map}.
nodes.label: def:non_co_map

nodes.label: def:self_adjoint_P

nodes.statement: We define a norm on $\mathcal{M}_D(\mathbb{C}) \otimes \mathbb{C} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_{r} \rangle$ by taking for a non-commutative polynomial with matrix coefficients $P \in \mathcal{M}_D(\mathbb{C}) \otimes \mathbb{C} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_{r} \rangle$, \begin{equation*} \|P\|_{D,r} := \sup \{ \|P(U_1, \ldots, U_r)\|, (U_i)_{1 \leq i \leq r} \text{ unitary matrices}\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:norm_non_comm_poly

nodes.statement: Let $r \geq 2$ and $D \geq 1$. Fix a self-adjoint non-commutative polynomial $P \in \mathcal{M}_D(\mathbb{C}) \otimes \mathbb{C} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_{r} \rangle$ of degree $q_0$, and let $K = \|P\|_{D,r}$. There exists a family of linear functionals $\nu_i : \mathcal{P} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ for $i \geq 0$ such that for every $N,m,q \geq 1$, and any $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$, \begin{equation*} \left|\mathbb{E}_{N,r}\left[\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))\right] - \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \frac{\nu_i(h)}{N^i}\right| \leq \frac{(4 q q_0(1+\log r))^{4m}}{N^m} \|h\|_{C^0([-K,K])}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: thm:masterI

nodes.statement: [todo]

nodes.statement: With the notations of Theorem \ref{thm:masterI}, for every $m, q \geq 1$ and $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$, \begin{equation*} |\nu_m(h)| \leq (4 q q_0(1+\log r))^{4m} \|h\|_{C^0([-K,K])}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: coro:masterI

nodes.statement:
Let $(F_N)_{N \geq 0}$ be a sequence. We assume there exists coefficients $(
u_i)_{i \geq 0}$, constants $(C_m)_{m \geq 1}$ and $(M_m)_{m \geq 1}$ such that, for all $m \geq 1$, all $N \geq M_m$,  egin{equation*} \left| F_N - \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}  rac{
u_i}{N^i} ight| \leq  rac{C_m}{N^m}. \end{equation*} Then, for all $m \geq 1$, $|
u_m| \leq C_m$.
nodes.label: lem:expansion_bound

nodes.statement: For any $h \in \mathcal{P}$, \begin{equation*} \nu_0(h) = \lim_{N \rightarrow +\infty} \mathbb{E}_{N,r} [\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))]. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:expr_nu_0

nodes.statement: Let $h \in \mathcal{P}$ and take $q \geq 1$ such that $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$. We apply Lemma \ref{lem:masterI_largeN} for $m=1$. Hence, for any $N \geq M$, \begin{equation*} \left| \mathbb{E}_{N,r} [\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))] - \nu_0(h) \right| \leq \frac{(4 q q_0(1+\log r))^4}{N} \end{equation*} The right-hand side goes to $0$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$, which leads to the claim.
For any $h \in \mathcal{P}$, any $N \geq 1$, \begin{equation*} |\mathbb{E}_{N,r} [\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))]| \leq \|h\|_{C^0([-K,K])}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:bound_trace

nodes.statement: Let $m \geq 0$, $q \geq 1$ and $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$. If $m=0$, by Lemma \ref{lem:expr_nu_0}, \begin{equation*} \nu_0(h) = \lim_{N \rightarrow +\infty} \mathbb{E}_{N,r} [\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))]. \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{lem:bound_trace}, this sequence is bounded by $\|h\|_{C^0([-K,K])}$, and in particular we get that at the limit $|\nu_0(h)| \leq \|h\|_{C^0([-K,K])}$. This is the claim for $m=0$. The result for $m \geq 1$ is a direct combination of Lemma \ref{lem:masterI_largeN} and Lemma \ref{lem:expansion_bound}.

With the notations of Theorem \ref{thm:masterI}, if $h$ is a constant polynomial, then \begin{itemize} \item $\nu_0(h)=h(0)$; \item for $i >0$, $\nu_i(h)=0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: lem:value_nu_at_one

nodes.statement: If $h$ is constant, then for any $N \geq 1$, $\mathbb{E}_{N,r}\left[\mathrm{tr}_{ND} h(P(S_1, \ldots, S_r))\right] = h(0)$ and the sequence from the claim satisfies the inequality from Theorem \ref{thm:masterI} and is hence the value of $(\nu_i(h))_{i \geq 0}$ by uniqueness [todo].

Let $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$. There exists a unique family of real numbers $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ such that, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{equation*} h(Kx) = \sum_{j=0}^q a_j T_j (x). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:chebyshev_decomp

nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that $h(Kx) \in \mathcal{P}_q$ and $(T_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_q$, since for all $0 \leq j \leq q$, $\deg T_j = j$.

Let $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$ and $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ be the coefficients from Lemma \ref{lem:chebyshev_decomp}. Let $f : \mathbb{T} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by $f(\theta) = h(K \cos \theta)$. Then, $f$ is an even trigonometric polynomial equal to \begin{equation*} f(\theta) = \sum_{j=0}^q a_j \cos(j \theta). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:f_def

nodes.statement: By definition of $f$ and $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$, for all $\theta \in \mathbb{T}$, \begin{equation*} f(\theta) = h(K \cos \theta) = \sum_{j=0}^q a_j T_j(\cos \theta). \end{equation*} By definition of $(T_j)_{j \geq 0}$, $T_j(\cos \theta) = \cos (j \theta)$. The evenness comes from the fact that $\cos$ is even.

Let $f(\theta) = \sum_{j=0}^q a_j \cos(j \theta)$ be an even trigonometric series. Then, the Fourier coefficients of $f$ are exactly, for $j \in \mathbb{Z}$, $c_j = \frac{1}{2} a_{|j|}$ if $0 < |j| \leq q$, $a_0$ if $j=0$ and $0$ if $|j|>q$.
nodes.label: lem:coeff_of_f

Let $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$ and $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ be the coefficients from Lemma \ref{lem:chebyshev_decomp}. Then, \begin{equation*} |a_0| \leq \| h \|_{C^0[-K,K]}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:bound_a0

nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:f_def} and \ref{lem:coeff_of_f}, we have \begin{equation*} a_0 = c_0 = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} f(\theta) \, \mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Hence by the triangle inequality \begin{equation*} |a_0| \leq \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} |f(\theta)| \, \mathrm{d} \theta = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} |h(K \cos \theta)| \, \mathrm{d} \theta \leq \| h \|_{C^0[-K,K]}. \end{equation*}

Let $1 < \beta \leq 2$ and $1/\beta_* = 1 - 1/\beta$. Let $f \in L^\beta(\mathbb{T})$ of Fourier coefficients $(c_j)_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$. Then, \begin{equation*} \left(\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} |c_j|^{\beta_*} \right)^{1/\beta_*} \leq \left(\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} |f(\theta)|^\beta \, \mathrm{d} \theta\right)^{1/\beta}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: thm:hausdorff_young

Let $\beta > 1$ and $1/\beta_* = 1-1/\beta$. Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ of Fourier coefficients $(c_j)_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$. Assume $f' \in L^\beta(\mathbb{T})$. Then, \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \neq 0} |c_j| \leq 4 \beta_* \|f' \|_{L^\beta(\mathbb{T})}. \end{equation*}

Let $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$, and $f$ and $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ be as in Lemma \ref{lem:f_def}. For any $m \geq 0$, any $\beta > 1$, if we denote $1/\beta_* := 1 - 1/\beta$, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{j=1}^q j^m |a_j| \leq 4 \beta_* \|f^{(m+1)}\|_{L^\beta(\mathbb{T})}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:bound_sum_aj

nodes.statement: First, we apply Lemma \ref{lem:coeff_of_f} to express the Fourier coefficients $(c_j)_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$ in terms of $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$. Let $m \geq 0$. By differentiation, the Fourier coefficients of $f^{(m)}$ satisfy, for all $j$, $c_j^{(m)} = i^m j^m c_j$. In particular, \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \neq 0} |c_j^{(m)}| = \sum_{j \neq 0} |j|^m |c_j| = \sum_{j =1}^q j^m |a_j|. \end{equation*} The conclusion follows by applying Lemma \ref{lem:Zygmund} to the function $f^{(m)}$, of derivative $f^{(m+1)}$ in $L^\beta(\mathbb{T})$ as it is a trigonometric polynomial and in particular smooth.

Let $m \geq 0$ be an integer and $K > 0$ be a real number. There exists a real number $c_{m,K}$ satisfying the following. For any $q \geq 1$, any $h \in \mathcal{P}_q$, if $(a_j)_{0 \leq j \leq q}$ are the coefficients from Lemma \ref{lem:chebyshev_decomp}, then \begin{equation*} \sum_{j=1}^q j^m |a_j| \leq c_{m,K} \|h\|_{C^{m+1}([-K,K])}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: coro:bound_sum_aj

nodes.statement: We apply Lemma \ref{lem:bound_sum_aj} with $\beta = \infty$, in which case $\beta_*=1$ and hence $$\sum_{j=1}^q j^m |a_j| \leq 4 \|f^{(m+1)}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T})}.$$ We then use the chain rule to find a constant $C_{m,K}$ such that $\|f^{(m+1)}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T})} \leq C_{m,K} \|h\|_{C^{m+1}([-K,K])}$ and conclude with $c_{m,K}=4C_{m,K}$.
Let $A$ be a subset of $\Omega$. We say $\nu \in \mathcal{D}'(\Omega, F)$ \emph{vanishes on} $A$ if, for all $h \in \mathcal{D}(\Omega, F)$, if $\mathrm{supp} \, h \subseteq A$, then $\nu(h)=0$.
nodes.label: def:distribution_vanishes

Let $
u \in \mathcal{D}'(\Omega, F)$. The \emph{support} of $
u$ is the intersection of all closed sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $
u$ vanishes on the complement of $A$. We denote it as $\mathrm{supp} \,

u(h)| \leq C \|h\|_{C^m(K)}$. But since $h$ is identically equal to $0$ outside of $K'$, $\|h\|_{C^m(K)} \leq \|h\|_{C^m(K')}$, which is what we needed to prove. Now to prove the support claim, let us prove that $
u$ vanishes on $K^c$, ie for all $h \in \mathcal{D}(\Omega,F)$ such that $\mathrm{supp} \, h \subseteq K^c$, we have $

u(h)=0$. Hence, the support of $
